steps.caption: White to move in an Exchange Variation middlegame. Before any words, count each side's pawns on the queenside (files a to d) and on the kingside (files e to h). Who has more where? What might that suggest about each side's plan?

claims.statement: d4 holds the white pawn.
d5 holds the black pawn.

steps.prompt: Make a guess before any explanation: which side is likely to push pawns on the queenside, and which on the kingside? Say why.

steps.text: **What you will be able to do.** Read the pawn skeleton of a Queen's Gambit position. Say which side holds the majority on which wing. Name the pawn break each side wants (a pawn move that challenges an enemy pawn). Test whether a break is ready by counting what supports it. Labels: [V] checked by counting or by the engine, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis, a guess worth testing.

steps.caption: The count. Queenside, files a to d: White has three pawns (a2, b2, d4), Black has four (a7, b7, c6, d5). Kingside, files e to h: White has four (e3, f2, g2, h2), Black has three (f7, g7, h7). Each side has a majority on one wing.

claims.statement: White has 3 pawns on the queenside.
Black has 4 pawns on the queenside.
Black's majority is the four pawns a7, b7, c6, d5.
White's majority is the four pawns e3, f2, g2, h2.

steps.caption: The same position, now the files. White has no c-pawn, so only Black's pawn stands on the c-file: it is half-open for White. Black has no e-pawn, so the e-file is half-open for Black. No file is fully open yet. Rooks go where files open.

claims.statement: No file is open; the c-file is half-open for White and the e-file for Black.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (game results, not evaluations). Source: our masters data, 329,379 games, both players rated 2500 or more. After the exchange on d5 and the bishop sortie to g5, Black played the pawn move c6 in 2,219 of 3,585 games and developed the bishop in 881. In the c6 games White won 786, 890 were drawn and Black won 543. Results also reflect who played.

steps.caption: Files are for rooks. In this position exactly two white moves put a rook on a half-open file, and both go to the c-file. Black's rook already stands on its half-open e-file.

line.say: The rook takes the half-open c-file and looks at the pawn on c6.

claims.statement: Exactly two legal moves, Rbc1 and Rfc1, put a white rook on a half-open file.

steps.text: **The minority attack, in plain words.** On the a, b and c files White has two pawns where Black has three. Pushing the b-pawn to b5 offers a trade. [I] Afterwards Black's remaining queenside pawns may be unable to defend each other. It fits when the pushed pawn is supported, Black has no faster threat, and White's pieces can reach the new target.

steps.caption: A model with pawns only, so nothing else distracts. Black's h-pawn moves stand in for moves Black makes elsewhere. Step through and watch the Black pawns on a7, b7, c6.

line.say: White starts the minority attack: the b-pawn heads for b5.
A waiting move. In a real game Black's pieces would do something here.
The pawn reaches b5 and attacks the pawn on c6.
Another waiting move.
White trades its b-pawn for Black's c6 pawn.
Black retakes. The structure has changed for good.

claims.statement: Before the push no black pawn is backward.
Before the push no black pawn is isolated.
After the trades the pawn on c6 is backward: its neighbour d5 is ahead and a white pawn attacks c5.
After the trades the pawn on a7 is isolated.
White's pawn on a2 is isolated as well.
The b-file is now open for both sides.

steps.text: **A target is not a won game.** A backward pawn matters only when your pieces can attack it and Black cannot cover it easily. White's own a-pawn is also isolated, and the open b-file serves both rooks. [I] Engines usually rate such positions as a small plus, not a win. The next board shows the same plan in a real opening line, with the engine's number attached.

steps.caption: From the opening line. The engine at depth 16 rates 12.b4 among its top choices here, level with the quiet 12.h3. The line is one plausible course, not the only one: Black could answer differently at every move.

Black puts the bishop on the diagonal towards h2.
The pawn arrives on b5, attacking c6 with three white pieces watching b5.
Black asks the bishop on g5 to decide.
White trades, as in the model.
Black retakes: c6 is backward and the b-file is open.

The pawn on h6 attacks the bishop on g5.

The b-file is open.

steps.caption: Black does not have to wait. Here Black has answered 12.b4 with ...a6, and White has backed up with a4. Black's best try is to trade pieces, starting with the knight move to e4, which attacks the bishop on g5.

White takes the bishop that guards e7 first.
Black retakes; one pair of bishops is gone.
The minority attack goes on: the pawn on b5 is defended four times (a4, Nc3, Bd3, Rb1) and attacked twice (a6, c6).
Black trades off a defender of b5.
White recaptures with the queen, which now eyes c6.

line.say: The plan starts as before.
Black attacks the pawn on b4 with the a-pawn.
White does not take. The pawn goes past, attacks c6 and cramps the black queenside.

steps.text: **Black's side [I].** Black's usual answers to the minority attack: trade pieces so fewer white pieces can use the new files, put a rook on the half-open e-file, and keep the knight ready for e4. ...a5 is not on this list because it lets b5 through. Black's own majority sits on the queenside, but it rarely advances in the middlegame. [H] Black's pawn majority matters mostly in endings, which is why Black avoids a queenless game with a weak c6.

steps.prompt: Which of these do you believe: (a) the minority attack is a real advantage, (b) it is only a pull on the position, (c) it depends entirely on the pieces? Say what in the boards made you choose.

steps.text: **The second break: e4.** [I] With a pawn on f3 behind it, a bishop on d3 and a knight on c3, the e-pawn can step to e4. It trades White's e-pawn for Black's d-pawn, opens the f-file for a rook, and makes a pair of pawns in the centre. It fits only when nothing important is left hanging while the pawn is in the air.

steps.text: **Two squares to check before any break.** Ask what Black's last move attacks. Then count the pawn that moves: how often it is attacked and how often defended. [I] A break that wins in one position can lose a piece in a position that differs by one knight move. The next three positions differ in exactly that way.

steps.caption: A plan is not always a break. In this position the engine's second choice is a quiet knight move that offers a trade of Black's most active piece. Two plans, both within half a pawn of the best.

Black takes.

steps.text: **Black's breaks.** In the non-exchange lines Black keeps e6 and d5 and often feels cramped: the bishop on c8 is shut in. Two pawn breaks free the position, ...e5 and ...c5. Each attacks White's pawn on d4. [I] Each needs preparation, and each leaves a recognisable structure behind. The next boards show the preparation first.

line.say: Trading pieces gives the rest more room.

steps.text: **Why the break waits.** [I] Black plays ...e5 only after the knights are traded and the pawn on e5 is defended as often as it is attacked. Before that, the knight on d5 leans on the pawn on e6 for support. Push the pawn and the knight loses a defender. The next board shows the punishment.

steps.caption: The same position as before, but now Black pushes at once. The knight on d5 was defended by the pawns on c6 and e6. Once the e-pawn moves, only the c-pawn defends it.

line.say: Black pushes without preparation.
White takes the knight: it is attacked twice and defended once.

claims.statement: After ...e5 the knight on d5 is attacked twice: Bc4 and Nc3.
After ...e5 the knight on d5 is defended once: c6.

steps.caption: Black recaptures, but the knight comes back with a threat. Look at where the knight on c3 lands.

line.say: Black recaptures the bishop.
The knight takes a pawn and attacks the queen on e7.

claims.statement: The knight on d5 attacks the queen on e7.
At depth 16 White is at least three pawns ahead after the line.

steps.text: **The other break: ...c5.** [I] When Black has fianchettoed the c8 bishop with ...b6 and ...Bb7, the pawn c5 strikes d4 from the other side. It does not threaten to win a pawn. It asks White what to do with the tension, and every answer changes the structure.

steps.caption: Black to move in the Tartakower setup. Black has a bishop on b7 aiming at the long diagonal and a pawn on d5 blocking it. Watch the c-pawn.

line.say: The break: the pawn on c5 attacks the pawn on d4.
White takes.
Black retakes with the b-pawn, opening the b-file for a rook.

claims.statement: At depth 16 c5 and Ne4 are both within 0.4 pawn of the best move.
After ...c5 the pawn on c5 attacks d4.
After the exchanges the b-file is half-open for Black.

steps.caption: Now White can release the tension again. If White takes on d5, Black gets a pair of pawns side by side in the centre.

line.say: White takes on d5 with the c-pawn.
Black retakes with the e-pawn.

claims.statement: After the exchange Black has hanging pawns on c5 and d5.
At depth 16 the engine sees White slightly ahead at most.

steps.caption: White need not take on c5. If White ignores the pawn, Black can trade on d4 and then on c4. A third structure appears.

line.say: The break, as before.
White waits and adds a rook to the d-file.
Black takes the pawn on d4.
White retakes with the e-pawn.
Black takes the pawn on c4.
White retakes with the bishop. The pawn on d4 now stands alone in the middle.

claims.statement: After the trades White's d4 pawn is isolated.
At depth 16 the position is within about half a pawn of level.

steps.text: **Two breaks, two kinds of structure.** [I] If White retakes with the e-pawn after ...e5, the result is an isolated pawn on d4 and an open e-file; retaking with the knight avoids that. After ...c5 the structure depends on White's answer: hanging pawns for Black if White takes on d5 with the c-pawn, an isolated pawn on d4 if White waits. Neither is good or bad in itself; it depends on whose pieces are more active. [H] Strong players may choose a break by the structure they prefer.

steps.prompt: Which structure would you rather play for a long game: Black's pair of hanging pawns, or White's lone pawn on d4? Pick one and give a reason from the boards.

steps.text: **Mixed tests.** Four positions follow with no hints about the theme. In each, check first what the opponent's last move attacks, then count what supports your break or plan. One of the four may need no break at all.

**Recap.**
- Count pawns by wing: each side usually has a majority on one wing.
- A half-open file belongs to the side with no pawn on it.
- A minority attack leaves a target, not a won game.
- White's central break needs a support pawn and a safe bishop.
- Black's breaks ...e5 and ...c5 wait until the pieces are ready.
- Before any break: what did the last move attack, and how often is the pawn attacked and defended?

**Self-check list for your teach-back.** Did you say when a break works and when it fails? Did you give an example a beginner could set up with a few pieces? Did you name one mistake, such as ...e5 without support or e4 with a loose bishop? Did you count how often the pawn is attacked and defended? Fix any gap before you write the final line.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine a friend who has never seen a Queen's Gambit structure. Write four short lines: the idea, when it works, one example you could set up on a board, one warning.
